newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran says two Bahais were Israeli spies.
newsitem.headline: Iran says two Bahais were Israeli spies.

text.p: Iran has denied that its courts sentenced two men to death because they followed the Bahai faith, describing Washington's version of the case as "utterly fabricated and spiteful."
The official news agency IRNA quoted the head of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Courts, Gholam Hoseyn Rahbarpour, as saying the two men were convicted of spying for Israel.
"No one in Iran will be prosecuted or punished for having a specific ideology or view," Rahbarpour said in the IRNA report late on Sunday.
The U.S. State Department last month condemned a decision by Iran's supreme court to uphold death sentences on two members of the Bahai faith and urged Tehran to release them.

Rahbarpour said: "The two that were sentenced to death were Musa Talebi and Zabihollah Mahrami. They were involved in espionage activities in the interests of Zionist aggressors. They were arrested while spying and were sentenced to death."
He said Iran's supreme court upheld the verdict, but Talebi was later pardoned. He gave no further details and it was not clear whether Mahrami had been executed.
Bahais in the United States say more than 200 members of their faith have been executed in Iran for their religious beliefs since the Islamic Revolution of 1979.

The Bahai faith, an offshoot of Islam, originated in Iran 150 years ago. It claims six million members worldwide, including 3,500 in Iran where it is officially considered "a misleading and wayward sect."
The State Department said the supreme court upheld death sentences passed on Talibi and Mahrami, who were convicted separately last year of "apostasy", a term used in Iran to denote abandoning Islam.
The United States had already appealed on behalf of the men when their original sentences were passed.
